\section{Appendix-only calibrated quotient, horizon, and fixed-radius corollaries}\label{sec:inverse}

This appendix uses the two response loci selected in
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main,thm:shells-general-main}. The default
physical comparison remains \Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main}; the quotient,
near-horizon, and fixed-radius statements collected here are additional
abstract calibrated toy-model corollaries obtained only after extra
calibration and ratio-data hypotheses are imposed. Appendix
Table~\ref{tab:hypothesis-ledger} summarizes that standing input. The boxed
quotient convention below fixes the notation once for the whole appendix
section and is not promoted into the main theorem narrative. Whenever a
spatial response profile has also been specified and the relevant range and
regularity conditions are verified, these same two loci may be described as the
corresponding regular spatial level-set pair. The
response loci use the same fixed switching convention as
Section~\ref{sec:kms-shells}, so switching enters only through
$\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2=\lambda_c^2\|\chi\|_2^2$.

\paragraph{Appendix reading order.}
Read the appendix from left to right:
\Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main} gives the fixed-response transport law,
\Cref{thm:ratio-main,prop:spectral-stability-main} add homogeneous or
slow-variation specializations, \Cref{lem:exact-collar-ratio-main,thm:horizon-main,cor:asymptotic-horizon-main}
add small-locus horizon algebra, and
\Cref{thm:two-mode-main,ass:ratio-data-clt-main,prop:two-mode-delta-main}
finally add the fixed-radius ratio map, the deterministic fixed-target
admissibility/local inverse corollary, and then the separate external-CLT
delta-method transport corollary.

\paragraph{Standing convention for this appendix section.}
Unless a later statement explicitly adds more structure, every result below
keeps Model~A together with the standing response-side package from
\Cref{ass:response-standing-main}. In particular, the fixed response profile
$R_\Omega$ is already chosen, the stationary spectrum is gap-regular and
absolutely continuous at $\pm\Omega$ with no atom there,
$\widehat W_x(\Omega)>0$, and $R_\Omega$ is positive $C^1$ on the region
under study. Appendix Table~\ref{tab:hypothesis-ledger} remains the central
scope map for how those shared hypotheses are specialized later. The result
statements in this section therefore restate only the extra assumptions that
genuinely change the conclusion: homogeneous or slowly varying spectral
weight, small-locus or horizon scaling, or externally supplied fixed-radius
ratio-data asymptotics.

\paragraph{Comparator boundary for the inverse corollaries.}
These quotient, near-horizon, and fixed-radius statements are conditional
algebra inside one fixed calibrated response model. They are not new
local-temperature observables in the sense of Mistry--Pinzul
\cite{MistryPinzul2024DiamondTemp}, and they are not a general causal
measurement framework in the sense of Oeckl
\cite{Oeckl2025CausalMeasurement}.

\subsection{Default transport and its abstract calibrated specializations}

The response-locus-pair ratio used below is a quotient of the two Planck
denominators, not a quotient of the two target rates. For radii
$r_\varphi$ and $r_{\mathrm{mem}}$ selected by the two response-locus
equations define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:denominator-convention-main}
D_\varphi=e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(r_\varphi)}-1,\qquad
D_{\mathrm{mem}}=e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(r_{\mathrm{mem}})}-1,\qquad
Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}=\frac{D_\varphi}{D_{\mathrm{mem}}}.
\end{equation}
The exact-clock condition contains the sampling factor $\Delta\tau$, whereas
the memory-transition condition is already a rate condition. Keeping these two
source equations in denominator form is what fixes the quotient below.

The two members of the pair use the same externally calibrated response setup:
the gap, coupling scale, detector profile, and field state are fixed, while the
classical counter mode is changed from ideal one-step blanking to the sampled
one-recovery-opportunity boundary-reset mode. The physically default comparison
keeps the two response-locus points distinct inside one fixed calibrated
response profile and therefore retains the spectral-weight transport factor.
Only after that fixed-response identity has been stated do we impose
the extra homogeneous specialization
$\mathcal S_x(\Omega)\equiv\mathcal S(\Omega)$ and pass to the later abstract
quotient, near-horizon, and fixed-radius corollaries.

\medskip
\noindent
\fbox{%
\parbox{\dimexpr\linewidth-2\fboxsep-2\fboxrule\relax}{%
\textbf{Convention for response-locus-pair quotients.}
The slash notation records numerator over denominator in the written order:
\[
Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}:=\frac{D_\varphi}{D_{\mathrm{mem}}},
\qquad
Q_{\mathrm{mem}/\varphi}:=\frac{D_{\mathrm{mem}}}{D_\varphi}
=Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}^{-1}.
\]
We abbreviate the detector-side constant by
\[
C_D:=\frac{\Delta\tau\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}{\log\varphi}.
\]
Thus the abstract homogeneous denominator quotient derived below from the
homogeneous source equations is $Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}=C_D$, while the
reciprocal target-rate quotient is
\[
\frac{\gamma_\varphi}{\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=Q_{\mathrm{mem}/\varphi}
=C_D^{-1}.
\]
}}%
\medskip

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: fixed-response transport identity]\label{cor:spectral-transport-main}
\ResponseStandingClause let $x_\varphi$ and $x_{\mathrm{mem}}$ be two points of
the same fixed calibrated response profile satisfying the present paper's
ideal-benchmark and memory-transition response-locus equations
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-transport-source-main}
\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S_{x_\varphi}(\Omega)\Delta\tau}
     {D_\varphi}
=\log\varphi,
\qquad
\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S_{x_{\mathrm{mem}}}(\Omega)}
     {D_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau),
\end{equation}
where
\[
D_\varphi=e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(x_\varphi)}-1,
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{mem}}=e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(x_{\mathrm{mem}})}-1.
\]
Then the fixed-response spectral-transport identity in the present notation is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-transport-main}
Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}
=\frac{D_\varphi}{D_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=
\frac{\Delta\tau\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}{\log\varphi}
\frac{\mathcal S_{x_\varphi}(\Omega)}
     {\mathcal S_{x_{\mathrm{mem}}}(\Omega)}
=C_D
\frac{\mathcal S_{x_\varphi}(\Omega)}
     {\mathcal S_{x_{\mathrm{mem}}}(\Omega)} .
\end{equation}
When the range and regularity hypotheses of
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main,thm:shells-general-main} hold at these externally
specified points and a spatial response profile has been supplied, the same
identity is the transport law along the corresponding regular spatial level
sets.  This identity does not estimate those points from the finite click
record.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
All factors in \eqref{eq:general-transport-source-main} are positive under the
standing response-side hypotheses. Solving the two source equations for the
Planck denominators gives
\[
D_\varphi=
\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S_{x_\varphi}(\Omega)\Delta\tau}
     {\log\varphi},
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{mem}}=
\frac{\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S_{x_{\mathrm{mem}}}(\Omega)}
     {\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}.
\]
Dividing the first expression by the second cancels the common switched detector
factor $\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2$ and gives \eqref{eq:spectral-transport-main}.
The final spatial-level-set sentence is only the substitution of the two
threshold loci from \Cref{thm:shells-general-main} into the regular-level-set
conclusion of \Cref{thm:response-locus-main}; no further detector-field input
is used.
\end{proof}

\Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main} is the starting identity for the rest of the
appendix. Everything below either cancels or perturbs its transport factor
under extra assumptions. Under the homogeneous input, the shared detector core
contributes one common positive factor
\[
\mathcal A=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)
\]
to both source response-locus equations.

Under the calibrated homogeneous spectral-weight regime and a common externally
calibrated response setup, the two source equations in the fixed denominator
notation are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:denominator-shells-main}
\frac{\mathcal A\Delta\tau}{D_\varphi}=\log\varphi,
\qquad
\frac{\mathcal A}{D_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau),
\qquad
\mathcal A=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)>0 .
\end{equation}
Here the ideal-benchmark member uses ideal one-step blanking, while the
memory-transition member uses the sampled one-recovery-opportunity
boundary-reset mode and the same sampling interval and recovery rate. Since all
factors are positive, these two source equations are equivalently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:denominator-rearranged-main}
D_\varphi=\frac{\mathcal A\Delta\tau}{\log\varphi},
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{mem}}=\frac{\mathcal A}{\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)} .
\end{equation}
The factor $\Delta\tau$ appears only in the ideal-benchmark source equation
because the ideal record threshold is $\Gamma\Delta\tau=\log\varphi$, whereas
the memory threshold is already a rate equation,
$\Gamma=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)$.
All quotient identities below are derived directly from the two displayed
source equations \eqref{eq:denominator-shells-main}--\eqref{eq:denominator-rearranged-main};
no unpublished homogeneous shell-ratio theorem is used as an input.

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: record-rate quotient from the homogeneous response-locus ratio]\label{thm:ratio-main}
\ResponseStandingClause assume in addition the calibrated homogeneous
spectral-weight regime and the local target-rate definitions
\eqref{eq:target-rates-main}. Then the two homogeneous source equations
\eqref{eq:denominator-shells-main} imply the denominator quotient
\[
Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}
=
\frac{D_\varphi}{D_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=
C_D,
\qquad
C_D=\frac{\Delta\tau\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}{\log\varphi},
\]
and the present paper's two record-selected target attempt rates obey
\begin{equation}\label{eq:target-quotient-main}
\frac{\gamma_\varphi}{\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=
Q_{\mathrm{mem}/\varphi}
=C_D^{-1}
=Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}^{-1}.
\end{equation}
This is a cancellation identity inside the calibrated homogeneous response
model; it does not derive the common amplitude $\mathcal A$ or the homogeneity of
$\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ from the KMS condition. For a general fixed calibrated
response function without the homogeneous specialization, the default physical
statement is instead \Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main}.
The proof below is included precisely to keep the quotient self-contained from
the displayed source equations, rather than importing a companion result.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Under the calibrated homogeneous spectral-weight regime and common-core
detector convention, both response-locus equations contain the same positive
amplitude
\[
\mathcal A=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)>0 .
\]
The source equations are precisely \eqref{eq:denominator-shells-main}. Solving
them gives \eqref{eq:denominator-rearranged-main}, namely
\[
D_\varphi=\frac{\mathcal A\Delta\tau}{\log\varphi},
\qquad
D_{\mathrm{mem}}
=\frac{\mathcal A}{\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)} .
\]
Both denominators are positive, so division is legitimate. Dividing the first
identity by the second cancels the common amplitude:
\[
Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}
=\frac{D_\varphi}{D_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=
\frac{\mathcal A\Delta\tau/\log\varphi}
     {\mathcal A/\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}
=
\frac{\Delta\tau\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}{\log\varphi}
=C_D .
\]
Independently, the target-rate definitions \eqref{eq:target-rates-main} give
\[
\frac{\gamma_\varphi}{\gamma_{\mathrm{mem}}}
=
\frac{\log\varphi/\Delta\tau}
     {\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}
=C_D^{-1}.
\]
Since
$Q_{\mathrm{mem}/\varphi}=D_{\mathrm{mem}}/D_\varphi
=Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}^{-1}$, this proves
\eqref{eq:target-quotient-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Self-contained quotient input]
The homogeneous denominator quotient $Q_{\varphi/\mathrm{mem}}=C_D$ is derived
above only from the two displayed source equations
\eqref{eq:denominator-shells-main}. No external spatial-geometry theorem is used
for the quotient law in this paper. The local bookkeeping consequence is that
the two target rates in \eqref{eq:target-rates-main} have the reciprocal
quotient \eqref{eq:target-quotient-main}.
\end{remark}

This appendix-only cancellation law uses one common field-facing core and
homogeneous spectral weight; without the second input the transport factor in
\Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main} remains. The sampling and recovery
parameters still enter through the readout constant
\[
C_D=\frac{\Delta\tau\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}{\log\varphi},
\]
so the ratio law is amplitude-free, not detector-free.

\begin{proposition}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: quantitative local homogeneity criterion]\label{prop:spectral-stability-main}
\ResponseStandingClause keep the same two response-locus points
and perturb only the spectral-weight homogeneity.
Assume the hypotheses
of \Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main}. Let $U$ be a geodesically convex
subset of the static slice containing $x_\varphi$ and $x_{\mathrm{mem}}$, and
suppose $\log \mathcal S_x(\Omega)$ is $C^1$ on $U$. Fix any auxiliary
Riemannian norm $|\cdot|$ on the slice and write
\[
L_U(\Omega)=\sup_{x\in U}|d\log \mathcal S_x(\Omega)|,
\qquad
d_U=d_U(x_\varphi,x_{\mathrm{mem}})
\]
for the corresponding geodesic distance between the two response-locus points. Let
\[
C_D=\frac{\Delta\tau\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)}{\log\varphi}
\]
and
\[
R=
\frac{e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(x_{\varphi})}-1}
     {e^{\beta_\infty\Omega N(x_{\mathrm{mem}})}-1}.
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-stability-main}
e^{-L_U(\Omega)d_U}
\le
\frac{\mathcal S_{x_\varphi}(\Omega)}
     {\mathcal S_{x_{\mathrm{mem}}}(\Omega)}
\le
e^{L_U(\Omega)d_U},
\end{equation}
and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq:spectral-stability-ratio-main}
C_D e^{-L_U(\Omega)d_U}
\le R\le
C_D e^{L_U(\Omega)d_U},
\qquad
\left|\frac{R}{C_D}-1\right|
\le e^{L_U(\Omega)d_U}-1.
\end{equation}
In particular, for any family with $L_{U_t}(\Omega(t))\,d_t\to0$ one has
\[
R(t)=C_D(t)\bigl(1+O(L_{U_t}(\Omega(t))\,d_t)\bigr).
\]
Thus the homogeneous ratio law is recovered asymptotically whenever the response-locus separation is small compared with the spatial variation scale of $\log\mathcal S_x(\Omega)$.
This is a deterministic spectral-weight perturbation estimate for the supplied
response profile; it is independent of the finite-record root-coordinate
instability at the exchange diagonal discussed in
\Cref{prop:finite-record-pre-diagonal-quotient-rule-main,cor:post-diagonal-no-label-reporting-main}.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let $\gamma:[0,d_U]\to U$ be a unit-speed minimizing geodesic from $x_{\mathrm{mem}}$ to $x_\varphi$. Then
\[
\log\frac{\mathcal S_{x_\varphi}(\Omega)}
         {\mathcal S_{x_{\mathrm{mem}}}(\Omega)}
=
\int_0^{d_U}
d\log\mathcal S_{\gamma(u)}(\Omega)\bigl[\dot\gamma(u)\bigr]\,du.
\]
Hence
\[
\left|
\log\frac{\mathcal S_{x_\varphi}(\Omega)}
         {\mathcal S_{x_{\mathrm{mem}}}(\Omega)}
\right|
\le
\int_0^{d_U}L_U(\Omega)\,du
=L_U(\Omega)d_U,
\]
which gives \eqref{eq:spectral-stability-main} after exponentiation. Combining
this estimate with the exact spectral-transport identity cited in
\Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main} yields
\eqref{eq:spectral-stability-ratio-main}. If $L_{U_t}(\Omega(t))d_t\to0$, then
$e^{L_{U_t}(\Omega(t))d_t}-1=O(L_{U_t}(\Omega(t))d_t)$, giving the final
estimate.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: uniform perturbative form]\label{cor:spectral-stability-perturbative-main}
\ResponseStandingClause the previous transport estimate
specializes as follows when the spectral weight is a uniform perturbation of a
homogeneous one.
Assume the hypotheses
of \Cref{prop:spectral-stability-main}. If, on the same region $U$,
\[
\mathcal S_x(\Omega)=\mathcal S(\Omega)(1+\varepsilon(x)),
\qquad
|\varepsilon(x)|\le\varepsilon_0<1,
\]
then
\[
C_D\,\frac{1-\varepsilon_0}{1+\varepsilon_0}
\le R\le
C_D\,\frac{1+\varepsilon_0}{1-\varepsilon_0},
\qquad
\left|\frac{R}{C_D}-1\right|
\le
\frac{2\varepsilon_0}{1-\varepsilon_0}.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By \Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main},
\[
\frac{R}{C_D}
=
\frac{1+\varepsilon(x_\varphi)}{1+\varepsilon(x_{\mathrm{mem}})}.
\]
The two-sided estimate follows by maximizing and minimizing the numerator and denominator under $|\varepsilon|\le\varepsilon_0$. The absolute bound follows from
\[
\left|
\frac{1+\varepsilon_\varphi}{1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mem}}}-1
\right|
=
\left|\frac{\varepsilon_\varphi-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mem}}}{1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{mem}}}\right|
\le
\frac{2\varepsilon_0}{1-\varepsilon_0}.
\]
\end{proof}

\subsection{Near-horizon corollaries inside the abstract calibrated specialization}

Near a nonextremal Hartle--Hawking horizon, the primary statement is the exact
collar identity for the homogeneous response-locus-pair denominator ratio
inside one fixed calibrated response profile. The proper-distance hierarchy
appears only after the extra small-gap condition
$\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\to0$ is imposed. Without that condition the valid
conclusion remains the exact nonlinear collar ratio. A Schwarzschild
specialization is recorded separately in Appendix~\ref{app:schwarzschild-toy}.

\begin{assumption}[Abstract calibrated toy-model hypothesis: small-locus horizon family]\label{ass:small-shell-main}
\ModelAClause a family of homogeneous response-locus
pairs is called \emph{small-locus} if it satisfies the following conditions.
A family of response-locus pairs in the abstract calibrated homogeneous specialization is called \emph{small-locus} if it is indexed by a parameter $t$, has detector gap $\Omega(t)>0$, and has proper distances
\[
\rho_\varphi(t)>0,\qquad \rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)>0
\]
from the horizon, satisfies the exact homogeneous ratio law
\[
\frac{e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t) N(\rho_\varphi(t))}-1}
     {e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t) N(\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t))}-1}
=C_D(t),
\qquad
C_D(t)=
\frac{\Delta\tau(t)\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r}(t),\Delta\tau(t))}
{\log\varphi},
\]
and obeys
\[
\epsilon(t)=\max\{\rho_\varphi(t),\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)\}\downarrow0 .
\]
The detector parameters may be fixed or may vary with $t$. The underlying fixed
response profile is still the one coming from the same gap-regular absolutely
continuous stationary response input as in \Cref{cor:homogeneous-main}, with no
atom or singular part at $\pm\Omega(t)$ along the family, strictly positive
one-gap density $\widehat W_x(\Omega(t))$, and a calibrated positive $C^1$
response profile on each fixed-$t$ region. The hypothesis is part of the
statement, not a consequence of the exact ratio law: outside such a family the
horizon expansion below is not being invoked. This assumption by itself gives
only an exact Planck-ratio relation in a normal collar. The linear
proper-distance law below is an additional consequence obtained only after the
dimensionless small-gap condition
$\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\to0$ is imposed.
\Cref{thm:response-locus-main,lem:abstract-homogeneous-specialization-main}
supply the response-level setting in which this family is interpreted.
\end{assumption}

\begin{lemma}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: near-horizon Planck denominator]\label{lem:varying-gap-denominator-main}
\ModelAClause assume the nonextremal horizon expansion
\[
N(\rho)=\kappa_{\mathrm H}\rho+O(\rho^3),
\qquad
\beta_\infty=\frac{2\pi}{\kappa_{\mathrm H}}.
\]
Let $\Omega(t)>0$, let $0<\rho(t)\le\epsilon(t)$, and suppose
$\epsilon(t)\downarrow0$. Then, uniformly for such $\rho(t)$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-near-horizon-denominator-main}
e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t)N(\rho(t))}-1
=
e^{2\pi\Omega(t)\rho(t)(1+O(\epsilon(t)^2))}-1 .
\end{equation}
If, in addition, $\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\to0$, then the denominator linearizes
uniformly:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:varying-gap-denominator-main}
e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t)N(\rho(t))}-1
=2\pi\Omega(t)\rho(t)
\Bigl(1+O(\Omega(t)\rho(t))+O(\rho(t)^2)\Bigr).
\end{equation}
In particular, if $\Omega(t)$ is bounded, the relative error is $O(\rho(t))$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The horizon expansion and the Hartle--Hawking relation give
\[
\beta_\infty\Omega(t)N(\rho)
=2\pi\Omega(t)\rho\bigl(1+O(\rho^2)\bigr),
\]
uniformly in a fixed normal collar. Since $\rho\le\epsilon(t)$ and
$\epsilon(t)\downarrow0$, this proves
\eqref{eq:exact-near-horizon-denominator-main}. If also
$\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\to0$, the exponent is $o(1)$ uniformly along the family.
Using $e^y-1=y(1+O(y))$ for $y=o(1)$ then gives
\[
e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t)N(\rho)}-1
=2\pi\Omega(t)\rho
\bigl(1+O(\rho^2)\bigr)
\bigl(1+O(\Omega(t)\rho)\bigr),
\]
which is \eqref{eq:varying-gap-denominator-main}. For bounded $\Omega(t)$ the
term $O(\Omega(t)\rho(t))$ is $O(\rho(t))$, while
$O(\rho(t)^2)$ is smaller.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: exact nonlinear near-horizon collar ratio]\label{lem:exact-collar-ratio-main}
\ModelAClause the exact homogeneous
response-locus-pair law has the following near-horizon collar form.
Assume the small-locus
horizon-family hypothesis in \Cref{ass:small-shell-main} and the nonextremal
Hartle--Hawking expansion
\[
N(\rho)=\kappa_{\mathrm H}\rho+O(\rho^3),
\qquad
\beta_\infty=\frac{2\pi}{\kappa_{\mathrm H}}.
\]
Then the exact homogeneous ratio law is equivalent to
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exact-collar-ratio-main}
C_D(t)=
\frac{
e^{2\pi\Omega(t)\rho_\varphi(t)(1+O(\epsilon(t)^2))}-1}
{
e^{2\pi\Omega(t)\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)(1+O(\epsilon(t)^2))}-1},
\end{equation}
with uniform $O(\epsilon(t)^2)$ terms along the family. This is the primary
near-horizon statement for small-locus families: it remains valid even when
$\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)$ does not tend to zero, and by itself it does not imply a
linear proper-distance or area-excess ratio.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply \Cref{lem:varying-gap-denominator-main} without the small-gap
linearization at $\rho_\varphi(t)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)$, then substitute
the exact homogeneous ratio law in \Cref{ass:small-shell-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: small-gap linearization of the exact collar ratio]\label{thm:horizon-main}
\ModelAClause assume in addition the homogeneous
small-locus horizon family and the dimensionless small-gap regime.
Assume the small-locus
horizon-family hypothesis in \Cref{ass:small-shell-main}, so that the
homogeneous response-locus pair comes from a
fixed calibrated response function $R_\Omega$, and the dimensionless
small-gap condition
\[
\eta(t):=\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\longrightarrow0 .
\]
Suppose that the static region ends at a nonextremal Hartle--Hawking horizon, so that $\beta_\infty=2\pi/\kappa_{\mathrm H}$ and, in proper distance $\rho$ from the horizon,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:horizon-main}
N(\rho)=\kappa_{\mathrm H}\rho+O(\rho^3)
\qquad(\rho\downarrow0).
\end{equation}
Then \Cref{lem:exact-collar-ratio-main} linearizes, and as
$\epsilon(t)\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:rho-ratio-main}
\frac{\rho_{\varphi}(t)}{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}
=
C_D(t)\Bigl(1+O(\eta(t))+O(\epsilon(t)^2)\Bigr).
\end{equation}
If the detector gap is fixed, or more generally uniformly bounded, this
estimate reduces to the simpler $O(\epsilon(t))$ relative-error form.
This is the small-gap linearization of
\Cref{lem:exact-collar-ratio-main}; without $\eta(t)\to0$ only the exact
nonlinear collar identity remains. \Cref{lem:high-gap-obstruction-main} gives
an explicit regime where the linear ratio fails. Appendix
~\ref{app:schwarzschild-toy} records the corresponding Schwarzschild
area-excess specialization.
\end{corollary}

Without the extra condition $\eta(t)=\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\to0$, the only valid
near-horizon conclusion is the exact collar ratio of
\Cref{lem:exact-collar-ratio-main}.

\begin{proof}
All estimates below are along the small-locus family, and the constants in the
$O(\cdot)$ terms are uniform after restricting to a sufficiently small normal
collar. Applying \Cref{lem:varying-gap-denominator-main} at
$\rho_\varphi(t)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)$ gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t) N(\rho_\varphi(t))}-1}
     {e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t) N(\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t))}-1}
&=
\frac{\rho_\varphi(t)}{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}
\frac{1+O(\Omega(t)\rho_\varphi(t))+O(\rho_\varphi(t)^2)}
     {1+O(\Omega(t)\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t))+O(\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)^2)}  \\
&=
\frac{\rho_\varphi(t)}{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}
\Bigl(1+O(\eta(t))+O(\epsilon(t)^2)\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The exact homogeneous ratio law says that the left-hand side is $C_D(t)$.
Hence
\[
C_D(t)=
\frac{\rho_\varphi(t)}{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}
\bigl(1+\delta(t)\bigr),
\qquad
\delta(t)=O(\eta(t))+O(\epsilon(t)^2).
\]
After restricting to $\epsilon(t)$ so small that $|\delta(t)|<1/2$,
$(1+\delta(t))^{-1}=1+O(\eta(t))+O(\epsilon(t)^2)$, which proves
\eqref{eq:rho-ratio-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: asymptotically homogeneous small-gap linearization]\label{cor:asymptotic-horizon-main}
\ModelAClause the homogeneous near-horizon
linearization remains valid under asymptotically homogeneous spectral
transport as follows.
Assume the same
calibrated horizon hypotheses as in \Cref{thm:horizon-main}, but replace exact
homogeneity by the
spectral-transport setting of \Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main}. Suppose the
shell points lie on the same static radial segment, define
\[
L_\epsilon(t)=\sup_{0\le \rho\le \epsilon(t)}
\left|\partial_\rho \log \mathcal S_\rho(\Omega(t))\right|,
\]
and assume in addition that
\[
L_\epsilon(t)\,\epsilon(t)\longrightarrow0 .
\]
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:asymptotic-rho-ratio-main}
\frac{\rho_{\varphi}(t)}{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}
=
C_D(t)\Bigl(1+O(\eta(t))+O(\epsilon(t)^2)+O(L_\epsilon(t)\epsilon(t))\Bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus the homogeneous small-gap linearization remains the leading term whenever
the response-locus separation shrinks faster than the spatial variation scale of
$\log \mathcal S_\rho(\Omega)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Because both shell points lie in $0\le\rho\le\epsilon(t)$ on the same radial segment, the one-dimensional mean-value estimate gives
\[
\left|
\log\frac{\mathcal S_{\rho_\varphi(t)}(\Omega(t))}
         {\mathcal S_{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}(\Omega(t))}
\right|
\le
L_\epsilon(t)\,|\rho_\varphi(t)-\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)|
\le
L_\epsilon(t)\,\epsilon(t).
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{\mathcal S_{\rho_\varphi(t)}(\Omega(t))}
     {\mathcal S_{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}(\Omega(t))}
=
1+O(L_\epsilon(t)\epsilon(t)).
\]
Combining this with the spectral-transport identity cited in
\Cref{cor:spectral-transport-main} yields
\[
\frac{e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t) N(\rho_\varphi(t))}-1}
     {e^{\beta_\infty\Omega(t) N(\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t))}-1}
=
C_D(t)\bigl(1+O(L_\epsilon(t)\epsilon(t))\bigr).
\]
Applying the proof of \Cref{thm:horizon-main} with this modified exact ratio replaces the left-hand side constant $C_D(t)$ by
$C_D(t)\bigl(1+O(L_\epsilon(t)\epsilon(t))\bigr)$, which gives
\eqref{eq:asymptotic-rho-ratio-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: high-gap obstruction to the linear ratio]\label{lem:high-gap-obstruction-main}
\ModelAClause assume the small-locus horizon-family hypotheses of
\Cref{ass:small-shell-main}. The condition
$\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\to0$ in
\Cref{thm:horizon-main} cannot be dropped. Suppose, along a small-locus
family, that
\[
\Omega(t)\epsilon(t)\to\Lambda\in(0,\infty),\qquad
\frac{\rho_\varphi(t)}{\epsilon(t)}\to a,\qquad
\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}(t)}{\epsilon(t)}\to b
\]
with $a,b\in(0,1]$. Then the exact collar ratio gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:high-gap-limit-main}
C_D(t)\longrightarrow
\frac{e^{2\pi\Lambda a}-1}{e^{2\pi\Lambda b}-1},
\end{equation}
whereas the proper-distance ratio tends to $a/b$. These two limits are not equal
in general.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Under the displayed hypotheses the correction
$O(\epsilon(t)^2)$ in \eqref{eq:exact-collar-ratio-main} contributes
$o(1)$ to the exponent, because
$\Omega(t)\rho_\star(t)O(\epsilon(t)^2)=O(\epsilon(t)^2)$ for
$\star\in\{\varphi,\mathrm{mem}\}$. Taking the limit in
\eqref{eq:exact-collar-ratio-main} gives \eqref{eq:high-gap-limit-main}. The
last assertion follows, for example, by taking $a\ne b$ and any fixed
$\Lambda>0$: the function $(e^{2\pi\Lambda x}-1)/x$ is not constant on
$(0,\infty)$.
\end{proof}

\Cref{lem:exact-collar-ratio-main} is the valid near-horizon statement before
linearization, \Cref{thm:horizon-main} is its extra small-gap linearization,
and \Cref{lem:high-gap-obstruction-main} shows why that hypothesis is
essential.

A particularly informative regime is the fast-sampling limit.
\begin{lemma}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: fast-sampling critical rate]\label{lem:fast-gammac-main}
\ModelAClause for fixed $\kappa_{\mathrm r}>0$ and $\Delta\tau\downarrow0$, equivalently $s=\kappa_{\mathrm r}\Delta\tau\downarrow0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fast-sampling-main}
\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{\mathrm r},\Delta\tau)
=
\frac{L+\log L+o(1)}{\Delta\tau},
\qquad
L=\log\frac{1}{s}.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $x=\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}/\kappa_{\mathrm r}$. The critical equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-c-main} is
\[
s=\frac{\log x}{x-1}.
\]
For $s\downarrow0$ the non-removable solution has $x\to\infty$. Put $x=(L+u)/s$, with $L=\log(1/s)$. Then
\[
\log x
=\log(L+u)-\log s
=L+\log(L+u),
\]
while
\[
s(x-1)=L+u-s.
\]
The equation $\log x=s(x-1)$ therefore becomes
\[
u=\log(L+u)+s .
\]
Since the right-hand side is $O(\log L)$, this identity first gives $u=O(\log L)$, and substituting back gives
$u=\log L+o(1)$. Hence
\[
\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}=\kappa_{\mathrm r}x
=\frac{s}{\Delta\tau}\frac{L+\log L+o(1)}{s}
=\frac{L+\log L+o(1)}{\Delta\tau}.
\]
\end{proof}

In the calibrated homogeneous near-horizon setting with fixed detector gap and response amplitude, both target rates diverge as $\Delta\tau\downarrow0$, so the corresponding lapse levels tend to zero. Thus the fast-sampling scaling produces a concrete algebraic small-locus family inside the homogeneous specialization of \Cref{thm:response-locus-main,lem:abstract-homogeneous-specialization-main}, rather than from a separately derived nonconstant-lapse UDW model, and it satisfies the dimensionless small-gap condition in Corollary~\ref{thm:horizon-main}. Combining that small-gap linearization with Lemma~\ref{lem:fast-gammac-main} gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fast-ratio-main}
\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{mem}}}{\rho_{\varphi}}
\sim
\frac{\log\varphi}{L+\log L}
\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Thus the memory-transition locus collapses toward the horizon parametrically faster than the ideal-benchmark locus. Whenever the regularity check is also verified, the corresponding shell pair therefore resolves a genuine hierarchy of stretched-horizon scales rather than two nearby realizations of the same thermal profile.

\subsection{Fixed-radius ratio-map corollaries inside the abstract calibrated specialization}

The fixed-radius material keeps the conservative object that the quotient
equations actually justify: one abstract ratio map at one fixed radius record.
The common response amplitude cancels from the ratio equations but remains a
separate admissibility variable in the undivided shell equations. Any
root-$N$ asymptotic law for nearby ratio data is supplied externally, not by
the single-setting click-record CLT of \Cref{thm:one-record-estimates-main}.

The Schwarzschild-specific toy specialization of the homogeneous ratio
equations, including the absolute-scale algebra and explicit admissibility
checks, is recorded separately in Appendix~\ref{app:schwarzschild-toy}. The
main text keeps only the fixed-radius ratio map that is justified directly by
the quotient equations.  AQFT/UDW communication work builds covariant
field-mediated channels \cite{KasprzakTjoa2025Transmission}; the construction
below is not such a channel or measurement theorem, but only calibrated
denominator-ratio bookkeeping after the fixed response model and radius record
have been specified. A related construction extends beyond any one
background family in a local ratio form. Each
detector operating mode supplies one response-locus pair and hence one scalar ratio
equation. Two genuinely distinct modes can provide two equations for a
two-parameter background family. The data objects used in those equations are
defined explicitly as follows. There are two different maps. The first is the
abstract fixed-radius ratio map
\[
\mathcal R_\eta:\Theta\to(0,\infty)^2,
\]
obtained after dividing within each detector mode. The second is the full
fixed-setting data map
\[
\mathcal F_\eta:\Theta\times(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)^4,
\]
which keeps the common unknown amplitude and the four undivided shell
equations. The inverse/sensitivity corollary below concerns only the abstract ratio map and
its local sensitivity to externally supplied nearby ratio data in
$(0,\infty)^2$; a physical shell record at the same fixed radii is encoded by the separate four-equation map
$\mathcal F_\eta$, which for fixed detector settings forces the single target
vector selected by those settings.

For later reference, the three data objects are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\eta &\quad \text{fixed radius record},\\
y &\in (0,\infty)^2 \quad \text{ratio datum at those fixed radii},\\
b &\in (0,\infty)^4 \quad \text{full fixed-setting shell target}.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the corollary below, the detector settings are held fixed, so $C$ and $b$ are
held fixed as well. Accordingly, a nearby point $y$ means nearby measured or
estimated denominator quotients for those same settings and that same radius
record $\eta_*$. It does not mean that the detector settings have been varied;
changing the settings would replace the constants $C_m$ and the target vector
$b$, hence would define a different inverse problem.

A two-mode radius record is written
\[
\eta=(\eta_{\varphi,1},\eta_{{\mathrm{mem}},1},
      \eta_{\varphi,2},\eta_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}).
\]
Here $J$ denotes the radial-coordinate interval for the chosen static spherical
coordinate convention. When radius records are varied only as ambient algebraic
variables, they are taken in an open set $\mathcal D\subset J^4$ on which the
response factors below are well defined, and the corresponding algebraic ratio
data lie in an open set $\mathcal E\subset\mathcal D\times(0,\infty)^2$.
For each $m$, the ideal-benchmark radius is obtained from ideal one-step
blanking with sampling interval $\Delta\tau_m$, while the memory radius is
obtained from the sampled one-recovery-opportunity boundary-reset mode and the
same sampling interval and recovery rate $\kappa_{{\mathrm r},m}$. The detector
settings supply the known physical ratio targets
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-mode-ratio-constants-main}
C_m=\frac{\Delta\tau_m\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{{\mathrm r},m},\Delta\tau_m)}{\log\varphi},
\qquad m=1,2.
\end{equation}

For a candidate background parameter $\theta$, define the two radius-dependent ratio observables
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-mode-ratio-functions-main}
R_m(\theta;\eta)=
\frac{e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{\varphi,m};\theta)}-1}
     {e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{{\mathrm{mem}},m};\theta)}-1},
\qquad
\mathcal R_\eta(\theta)=(R_1(\theta;\eta),R_2(\theta;\eta)).
\end{equation}
The physical residuals are
\[
H_m(\theta,\eta)=R_m(\theta;\eta)-C_m,\qquad
H(\theta,\eta)=\mathcal R_\eta(\theta)-C,
\]
where $C=(C_1,C_2)$.
If one physically estimates the two denominator quotients at the fixed radii
and detector settings, the resulting datum is a point
$\widehat y\in(0,\infty)^2$ approximating $\mathcal R_\eta(\theta)$. Thus a
nearby point of ratio space means a pair of nearby measured denominator
quotients for those same fixed radii and readout settings, not a perturbed
radius quadruple. Equivalently, the local inverse corollary below takes as input
estimated ratio data
\[
\widehat y\approx\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta_*)
\]
at one fixed radius record $\eta_*$ and one fixed pair of detector settings.
The paper does not derive such ratio data from the click-record diagnostics of
\Cref{sec:records} or from the shell-location equations alone. The covariance
statement later in this subsection is conditional on an external asymptotic law
for that ratio datum, and a subsequent remark records one standard delta-method
route by which shell-location or denominator estimators could supply it.
When those settings are kept fixed, exact full shell data are not a nearby
two-parameter family in ratio space: they still correspond only to the single
physical target $C$ in the ratio projection of the four-equation map
$\mathcal F_{\eta_*}$.

The full shell bookkeeping is separate from the two ratio equations. Let
\[
\mathcal A=\lambda_{\mathrm{sw}}^2\mathcal S(\Omega)
\]
denote the unknown homogeneous hardware prefactor. For a candidate background
parameter $\theta$, radius record $\eta$, and mode $m$, the undivided shell
equations define the amplitude values
\[
\mathcal A_{\varphi,m}(\theta;\eta)=
\frac{\log\varphi}{\Delta\tau_m}
\bigl(e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{\varphi,m};\theta)}-1\bigr),
\]
and
\[
\mathcal A_{{\mathrm{mem}},m}(\theta;\eta)=
\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{{\mathrm r},m},\Delta\tau_m)
\bigl(e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{{\mathrm{mem}},m};\theta)}-1\bigr).
\]
Equivalently, for fixed $\eta$ the full undivided shell data are encoded by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:full-fixed-radius-map-main}
\mathcal F_\eta(\theta,\mathcal A)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{\mathcal A\Delta\tau_1}
      {e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{\varphi,1};\theta)}-1} \\
\dfrac{\mathcal A}
      {e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{{\mathrm{mem}},1};\theta)}-1} \\
\dfrac{\mathcal A\Delta\tau_2}
      {e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{\varphi,2};\theta)}-1} \\
\dfrac{\mathcal A}
      {e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{{\mathrm{mem}},2};\theta)}-1}
\end{pmatrix},
\end{equation}
with target vector
\begin{equation}\label{eq:full-fixed-radius-target-main}
b=
\bigl(
\log\varphi,\,
\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{{\mathrm r},1},\Delta\tau_1),\,
\log\varphi,\,
\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{{\mathrm r},2},\Delta\tau_2)
\bigr).
\end{equation}
Thus $\eta$ is a full common-core shell record exactly when there exist
$(\theta,\mathcal A)$ with $\mathcal A>0$ such that
$\mathcal F_\eta(\theta,\mathcal A)=b$. Dividing the first pair and the second
pair of entries in \eqref{eq:full-fixed-radius-map-main} eliminates
$\mathcal A$ and leaves the two ratio equations
$\mathcal R_\eta(\theta)=C$.

\begin{lemma}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: ratio residuals and full common-core data]\label{lem:ratio-admissibility-main}
\ResponseStandingClause the ratio equations and the full
shell-data equations are related as follows at fixed detector settings.
For a fixed physical mode $m$, candidate parameter $\theta$, and radius record
$\eta$, the equation $H_m(\theta,\eta)=0$ is equivalent to the within-mode
amplitude equality
\[
\mathcal A_{\varphi,m}(\theta;\eta)=\mathcal A_{{\mathrm{mem}},m}(\theta;\eta).
\]
The pair of ratio equations $H(\theta,\eta)=0$ contains no unknown
$\mathcal A$. A radius record is an exact full common-core shell record at the
same $\theta$ only if, in addition, the four estimates
\[
\mathcal A_{\varphi,1},\quad \mathcal A_{{\mathrm{mem}},1},\quad
\mathcal A_{\varphi,2},\quad \mathcal A_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}
\]
are all positive and equal to one common value $\mathcal A>0$, and the four
radii lie in the exterior coordinate ranges of the background family.
Equivalently, the abstract ratio condition $H(\theta,\eta)=0$ becomes a
physical fixed-radius shell solution only after the full map in
\eqref{eq:full-fixed-radius-map-main} hits the target vector
\eqref{eq:full-fixed-radius-target-main}. These extra conditions are not
consequences of the ratio equations. In particular, once the detector settings
and hence the target vector $b$ are fixed, every exact full common-core shell
solution satisfies
\[
\mathcal R_\eta(\theta)=C.
\]
Therefore a nearby point $y\neq C$ has no exact interpretation as full
fixed-setting shell data unless one explicitly changes the detector targets
themselves or treats $y$ only as an estimated ratio datum in the abstract ratio
space.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By the definitions above,
\[
\frac{\mathcal A_{\varphi,m}(\theta;\eta)}
{\mathcal A_{{\mathrm{mem}},m}(\theta;\eta)}
=
\frac{e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{\varphi,m};\theta)}-1}
     {e^{\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(\eta_{{\mathrm{mem}},m};\theta)}-1}
\frac{\log\varphi}
{\Delta\tau_m\,\Gamma_{\mathrm{crit}}(\kappa_{{\mathrm r},m},\Delta\tau_m)}
=\frac{H_m(\theta,\eta)+C_m}{C_m}.
\]
Thus $H_m(\theta,\eta)=0$ is exactly the equality of the two within-mode
amplitude estimates. The formula for $H_m$ contains only the radius record, the
background family, the gap, and the readout constants; the common prefactor
$\mathcal A$ has cancelled. Equality across the two modes, positivity, and the
exterior-range restrictions are separate requirements. They cannot be inferred
from $H(\theta,\eta)=0$, because the ratio operation has deliberately discarded
the absolute scale and does not encode the allowed radial range. In
\eqref{eq:full-fixed-radius-map-main}, that discarded scale is exactly the
unknown common amplitude $\mathcal A$. Conversely, if
$\mathcal F_\eta(\theta,\mathcal A)=b$ for some $\mathcal A>0$, then dividing
the first and second entries and also the third and fourth entries recovers
$R_m(\theta;\eta)=C_m$ for $m=1,2$, hence $\mathcal R_\eta(\theta)=C$.
\end{proof}

\begin{assumption}[Abstract calibrated toy-model hypothesis: external ratio-data CLT at fixed radii]\label{ass:ratio-data-clt-main}
\ResponseStandingClause the statistical input for the fixed-radius
inverse statement is the following external ratio-data asymptotic law. This is
an appendix-level assumption, not a consequence of the fixed-setting long-record theorem in
\Cref{sec:records}: the record-side quotient inverse estimates only the
visible sampled-counter survival factors from the three inclusion coordinates,
while the fixed-radius problem below needs denominator quotients tied to
response locations.  The record theorem supplies no denominator, location, or
fixed-radius response-ratio CLT.
Assume the calibrated homogeneous fixed-radius setting inherited from
\Cref{thm:ratio-main}. Let $\Theta\subset\RR^2$ be open, let $J$ be the radial
interval used by a fixed static spherical coordinate chart, and suppose
\[
N:J\times\Theta\to(0,\infty),
\qquad
\beta_\infty:\Theta\to(0,\infty)
\]
are $C^1$. Choose a fixed radius record
\[
\eta_*=(r_{\varphi,1},r_{{\mathrm{mem}},1},
        r_{\varphi,2},r_{{\mathrm{mem}},2})\in J^4
\]
on which the ratio functions in \eqref{eq:two-mode-ratio-functions-main} are
defined, and keep the same detector settings and hence the same fixed targets
$C=(C_1,C_2)$ and $b$ from
\eqref{eq:two-mode-ratio-constants-main} and
\eqref{eq:full-fixed-radius-target-main}. Assume that this record comes from
admissible full common-core shell data at $\theta_*$ with one positive shared
amplitude $\mathcal A_*>0$, so that
\[
\mathcal F_{\eta_*}(\theta_*,\mathcal A_*)=b
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta_*)=C
\]
and
\[
\mathcal A_{\varphi,1}(\theta_*;\eta_*)
=\mathcal A_{{\mathrm{mem}},1}(\theta_*;\eta_*)
=\mathcal A_{\varphi,2}(\theta_*;\eta_*)
=\mathcal A_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}(\theta_*;\eta_*)
=\mathcal A_*>0,
\]
with all four radii lying in the exterior coordinate range at $\theta_*$. Let
$\widehat y_N\in(0,\infty)^2$ be externally supplied estimated ratio data for
those fixed detector settings and that fixed radius record. These data are not
claimed here to be produced by the click-record diagnostics or by the shell
equations alone; they are an additional input to the fixed-radius inverse
problem. Assume that
\[
\sqrt{N}\,(\widehat y_N-C)\Longrightarrow \mathcal N(0,\Sigma_y)
\]
for some positive semidefinite $2\times2$ matrix $\Sigma_y$. In particular,
\[
\widehat y_N=C+O_{\mathbb P}(N^{-1/2}),
\]
so any later inverse branch is applied only to estimated denominator quotients
centered at the exact fixed-setting target. The stochastic content of this
assumption is exactly the displayed ratio-data CLT; no part of it is imported
from \Cref{lem:finite-lag-renewal-reward-main} or \Cref{thm:one-record-estimates-main}. The
identities above merely fix the exact base point
$(\theta_*,\mathcal A_*,\eta_*,C,b)$ for the deterministic fixed-radius
statements below.
\end{assumption}

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: fixed-target admissibility and local ratio inverse at fixed radius]\label{thm:two-mode-main}
\ResponseStandingClause this fixed-radius corollary is deterministic. It uses only
the exact fixed-target base point singled out in
\Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main}, not the external ratio-data CLT itself. Set
\[
\mathcal R_*=\mathcal R_{\eta_*}.
\]
Assume, in addition, that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two-mode-ratio-jacobian-main}
\det D_\theta\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta_*)\neq0.
\end{equation}
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.25em]
\item Exact full common-core shell data at these same fixed settings remain
pinned to the single physical ratio target $C$. More precisely, for any
$\theta\in\Theta$ and any $\mathcal A>0$,
\[
\mathcal F_{\eta_*}(\theta,\mathcal A)=b
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta)=C.
\]
\item There are neighbourhoods $U\subset\Theta$ of $\theta_*$ and
$Y\subset(0,\infty)^2$ of $C$, together with a unique $C^1$ branch
\[
\mathcal I_{\eta_*}:Y\to U,\qquad \mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)=\theta_*,
\]
such that
\[
\mathcal R_*(\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(y))=y\qquad(y\in Y).
\]
If $\theta\in U$ and $\mathcal R_*(\theta)=y\in Y$, then
$\theta=\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(y)$.
\item If $\theta\in U$ and $\mathcal A>0$ satisfy
\[
\mathcal F_{\eta_*}(\theta,\mathcal A)=b,
\]
then necessarily
\[
\theta=\theta_*,
\qquad
\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta)=C.
\]
Consequently every nearby point $y\in Y\setminus\{C\}$ is only an abstract
ratio-space datum for the same fixed-setting inverse problem. It is not exact
full shell data at the fixed record $\eta_*$ and the same detector settings.
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Part (i) is exactly the fixed-target consequence of
\Cref{lem:ratio-admissibility-main}: if
$\mathcal F_{\eta_*}(\theta,\mathcal A)=b$ for some $\mathcal A>0$, then
$\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta)=C$. The displayed exact shell identity at
$(\theta_*,\mathcal A_*)$ is part of the fixed-base-point setup recorded above,
so exact full common-core shell data at the fixed settings occur only at the
single physical ratio target $C$.

For the inverse branch in part (ii), the stated regularity makes
$\mathcal R_*:\Theta\to\RR^2$ a $C^1$ map with exact base point
$\mathcal R_*(\theta_*)=C$. To make the Jacobian condition explicit, write
\[
B_{\varphi,m}(\theta)=\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(r_{\varphi,m};\theta),
\qquad
B_{\mathrm{mem},m}(\theta)=\beta_\infty(\theta)\Omega N(r_{{\mathrm{mem}},m};\theta).
\]
Then
\[
d_\theta R_m=
\frac{
e^{B_{\varphi,m}}\,d_\theta B_{\varphi,m}\,(e^{B_{\mathrm{mem},m}}-1)
-(e^{B_{\varphi,m}}-1)e^{B_{\mathrm{mem},m}}\,d_\theta B_{\mathrm{mem},m}
}
{(e^{B_{\mathrm{mem},m}}-1)^2}.
\]
Thus \eqref{eq:two-mode-ratio-jacobian-main} is the concrete requirement that
the two row covectors supplied by the two fixed-radius ratio equations are not
collinear at $\theta_*$. Apply the ordinary inverse function theorem to
$\mathcal R_*$ at $\theta_*$. This yields neighbourhoods $U,Y$ and the unique
$C^1$ inverse branch $\mathcal I_{\eta_*}$. Exterior admissibility of the fixed
record is an open condition in $\theta$, so $U$ may be shrunk if necessary to
keep the fixed radii in the allowed coordinate range throughout $U$.

For part (iii), combine part (i) with the uniqueness statement in part (ii).
If $\theta\in U$ and $\mathcal F_{\eta_*}(\theta,\mathcal A)=b$ for some
$\mathcal A>0$, then part (i) gives $\mathcal R_*(\theta)=C$, hence
$\theta=\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)=\theta_*$. The final sentence is just this local
uniqueness restated in the ratio-space variable: points
$y\in Y\setminus\{C\}$ parametrize nearby abstract ratio values, not nearby
exact fixed-target shell records.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Abstract calibrated toy-model corollary: delta-method transport for fixed-radius ratio estimates]\label{prop:two-mode-delta-main}
\ResponseStandingClause this statistical fixed-radius corollary starts only after
the deterministic inverse branch of \Cref{thm:two-mode-main} and the external
ratio-data CLT of \Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main} have both been supplied. It is
therefore a conditional delta-method transport statement for externally supplied
ratio data, not a corollary of the one-record regenerative CLT and not a
field-mediated communication construction of the kind studied in
\cite{KasprzakTjoa2025Transmission}. Let
$U$, $Y$, and $\mathcal I_{\eta_*}:Y\to U$ be the neighbourhoods and inverse
branch from \Cref{thm:two-mode-main}. Define
\[
\widehat\theta_N=
\begin{cases}
\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(\widehat y_N),& \widehat y_N\in Y,\\
\theta_*,& \widehat y_N\notin Y.
\end{cases}
\]
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.2em,itemsep=0.25em]
\item One has
\[
\sqrt{N}\,(\widehat\theta_N-\theta_*)
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_\theta),
\]
with
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delta-covariance-main}
\Sigma_\theta
=D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)\,\Sigma_y\,D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)^\top
=\bigl[D_\theta\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta_*)\bigr]^{-1}
\Sigma_y
\bigl[D_\theta\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta_*)\bigr]^{-{\top}}.
\end{equation}
\item If $\widehat\Sigma_{y,N}\to\Sigma_y$ in probability and one sets
\[
\widehat\Sigma_{\theta,N}=
\begin{cases}
D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(\widehat y_N)\,
\widehat\Sigma_{y,N}\,
D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(\widehat y_N)^\top,& \widehat y_N\in Y,\\
0,& \widehat y_N\notin Y,
\end{cases}
\]
then
\[
\widehat\Sigma_{\theta,N}\to\Sigma_\theta
\qquad\text{in probability}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Because \Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main} gives
$\widehat y_N=C+O_{\mathbb P}(N^{-1/2})$ and $Y$ is a neighbourhood of $C$,
\[
\mathbb P(\widehat y_N\in Y)\to1.
\]
Hence the auxiliary values assigned outside $Y$ are asymptotically negligible.
Apply the multivariate delta method to the $C^1$ map
$\mathcal I_{\eta_*}$ at the point $C$ using the external CLT from
\Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main}. This gives
\[
\sqrt{N}\,(\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(\widehat y_N)-\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C))
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal N\!\bigl(0,
D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)\Sigma_y D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)^\top\bigr).
\]
Since $\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)=\theta_*$, this is the stated Gaussian limit for
$\widehat\theta_N$. The identity
\[
D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(C)=\bigl[D_\theta\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta_*)\bigr]^{-1}
\]
is the chain rule for the local inverse branch, yielding
\eqref{eq:delta-covariance-main}. Part (ii) follows from the continuity of
$D\mathcal I_{\eta_*}$ on $Y$, the convergence
$\widehat y_N\to C$ in probability, and Slutsky's theorem. No ratio-data
asymptotic is proved inside this corollary; all stochastic input comes from
\Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[One sufficient source of the ratio-data CLT]\label{rem:ratio-data-delta-source-main}
One standard route to \Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main} is external to the
fixed-setting long-record theorem: start from an
external estimator of the positive denominator vector
\[
D_*=(D_{\varphi,1}^*,D_{{\mathrm{mem}},1}^*,D_{\varphi,2}^*,D_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}^*)
\in(0,\infty)^4,
\]
for which
\[
C_1=\frac{D_{\varphi,1}^*}{D_{{\mathrm{mem}},1}^*},
\qquad
C_2=\frac{D_{\varphi,2}^*}{D_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}^*}.
\]
If an external procedure supplies estimators $\widehat D_N$ satisfying
\[
\sqrt{N}\,(\widehat D_N-D_*)\Longrightarrow\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_D),
\]
and one forms the ratio datum by
\[
\widehat y_N=G(\widehat D_N),\qquad
G(d_{\varphi,1},d_{{\mathrm{mem}},1},d_{\varphi,2},d_{{\mathrm{mem}},2})
=\left(\frac{d_{\varphi,1}}{d_{{\mathrm{mem}},1}},
\frac{d_{\varphi,2}}{d_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}}\right),
\]
then the multivariate delta method yields
\[
\sqrt{N}\,(\widehat y_N-C)\Longrightarrow \mathcal N(0,\Sigma_y),
\qquad
\Sigma_y=DG(D_*)\,\Sigma_D\,DG(D_*)^\top,
\]
with
\[
DG(D_*)=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{1}{D_{{\mathrm{mem}},1}^*}
&
-\dfrac{D_{\varphi,1}^*}{(D_{{\mathrm{mem}},1}^*)^2}
& 0 & 0\\[1.1ex]
0 & 0 &
\dfrac{1}{D_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}^*}
&
-\dfrac{D_{\varphi,2}^*}{(D_{{\mathrm{mem}},2}^*)^2}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The same composition principle applies if one first proves a CLT for external
shell-location or lapse estimators and then passes to the denominators and
their quotients through the smooth maps in
\eqref{eq:two-mode-ratio-functions-main}. The present paper does not prove such
an external CLT; it records only the conditional inverse/sensitivity consequences once
that input is available. In particular,
\Cref{thm:one-record-estimates-main} already isolates why the single-record CLT
for $\gamma_2$ is insufficient for these ratio coordinates.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[External localization route to the ratio-data CLT]\label{prop:ratio-data-shell-source-main}
The same external input can arise from a localization protocol, but
that derivation is separate from, and not implied by, the one-record CLT proved in
\Cref{sec:records}. Keep the same fixed detector settings, the same exact
radius record $\eta_*\in J^4$, and the same background parameter
$\theta_*\in\Theta$ from \Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main}. Define the
fixed-parameter ratio map in the radius variables by
\[
h:\mathcal D\to(0,\infty)^2,
\qquad
h(\eta)=\mathcal R_\eta(\theta_*),
\]
on an open neighborhood $\mathcal D\subset J^4$ of $\eta_*$. Suppose an
external localization procedure supplies response-locus position estimators
$\widehat\eta_N\in\mathcal D$ such that
\[
\sqrt N\,(\widehat\eta_N-\eta_*)
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_\eta)
\]
for some positive semidefinite $4\times4$ matrix $\Sigma_\eta$. Then the
derived ratio datum
\[
\widehat y_N=h(\widehat\eta_N)
\]
satisfies
\[
\sqrt N\,(\widehat y_N-C)
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal N(0,\Sigma_y),
\qquad
\Sigma_y=
D_\eta h(\eta_*)\,\Sigma_\eta\,D_\eta h(\eta_*)^\top.
\]
Because $h(\eta_*)=\mathcal R_{\eta_*}(\theta_*)=C$, this is exactly one
sufficient protocol-level route to the external input assumed in
\Cref{ass:ratio-data-clt-main}. The present paper does not prove such a
localization CLT; it records only that, once supplied, the inverse-function
algebra of \Cref{prop:two-mode-delta-main} transports it to parameter space.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Inverse-branch meaning versus retuned exact targets]\label{rem:fixed-target-versus-retuned-main}
The interpretation of
\Cref{thm:two-mode-main,prop:two-mode-delta-main} is strictly fixed-setting.
Once the detector settings and the radius record $\eta_*$ are frozen, the ratio
target is the single point $C=(C_1,C_2)$ and the undivided shell target is the
single vector $b$. The deterministic corollary \Cref{thm:two-mode-main} says
that exact fixed-setting shell data at those same settings still occur only at
$y=C$, while the statistical corollary \Cref{prop:two-mode-delta-main} uses the
same inverse branch only for nearby observed denominator quotients $y$.

If one instead wants nearby $y$ to represent exact shell data, the detector
targets must vary with $y$. In the present notation the corresponding
$y$-dependent target vector is
\[
b(y)=
\left(
\log\varphi,\,
\frac{y_1\log\varphi}{\Delta\tau_1},\,
\log\varphi,\,
\frac{y_2\log\varphi}{\Delta\tau_2}
\right),
\]
because the exact within-mode quotient relation is
$y_m=\Delta\tau_m\Gamma_{{\mathrm{crit}},m}/\log\varphi$. The exact equation in
that retuned problem is then
\[
\mathcal F_{\eta_*}(\mathcal I_{\eta_*}(y),\mathcal A(y))=b(y),
\]
which is a different retuned-target calibration problem from the fixed-setting inverse problem
treated in \Cref{thm:two-mode-main,prop:two-mode-delta-main}.
\end{remark}

If one instead varies the radius quadruple as an ambient algebraic parameter,
the corresponding residual graph and the restriction to full common-core shell
data are recorded separately in
\Cref{cor:ambient-ratio-graph-app-main,thm:full-shell-subset-main,cor:full-shell-restriction-main}. Those appendix statements describe the local geometry of the ratio residual equations in the enlarged data space; they are not local ratio-map inverse theorems from nearby shell records to background geometry.

Appendix~\ref{app:schwarzschild-toy} records a separate Schwarzschild toy
specialization of this fixed-radius algebra, including the one-parameter
Hartle--Hawking branch reduction and a worked table. It remains explicit
calibrated-model bookkeeping rather than an exact nonconstant-lapse
detector-field construction.

\begin{remark}\label{rem:jacobian-main}
The Jacobian condition~\eqref{eq:two-mode-ratio-jacobian-main} is the local regularity condition for the ratio-map inverse branch, evaluated at the exact radius record and physical ratio target. It can fail because the two modes produce redundant ratio functions, or because the chosen background parametrization affects the two recorded radii in linearly dependent ways. Equality $C_1=C_2$ is therefore not a complete degeneracy criterion; it is a warning sign that the two modes may not provide independent constraints. Choosing distinct sampling and recovery parameters is necessary in practice, but the determinant in~\eqref{eq:two-mode-ratio-jacobian-main} is the actual inverse-regularity test.
\end{remark}

# Feasibility note: n-state killed-reset D-MAP identifiability

## Decision

A universal labelled-kernel inverse is false, but a sharp minimal-class
dichotomy is attainable. Deterministic reset reduces the visible law to the
scalar Palm tail S_k = e_n^T K^k 1. Standard minimal realization theory says
that two rank-n representations of this sequence differ by a unique
similarity preserving 1 and e_n^T. Therefore a declared subclass is
identifiable, up to its allowed state relabellings, exactly when the
intersection of each such similarity orbit with the subclass's nonnegative
substochastic cone has one declared structural-equivalence class.

This orbit--cone criterion is necessary and sufficient, but its realization
input is established theory rather than a new general phase-type theorem.
The new model-specific conclusion is the location of two opposite classes:

- every minimal interior point of the unrestricted killed-reset cone has a
  continuum visible fibre;
- the pure serial absorption subclass identifies the unordered rate multiset
  for all positive rates, including repeated rates.

Pole collision is therefore not the identifiability boundary. In the serial
model it produces confluent Prony terms and singular finite-sample root
coordinates, while algebraic multiplicity still identifies the repeated rate
at population level. The boundary is the Markovian orbit fibre.

## Scope

The theorem assumes minimal/Hankel rank n. Lower-rank nominal n-state
representations require a separate stratified augmentation theory. For an
arbitrary fixed nonserial zero pattern, deciding the orbit--cone intersection
remains a graph-specific semialgebraic problem. These limitations are explicit
open interfaces in the manuscript.

## Machine evidence

verify_nstate_identifiability.py evaluates representative n=2,3,4 serial
models, including repeated sampled poles. It computes Palm tails and stationary
click moments, reconstructs the order-n Hankel recurrence, verifies full
Hankel rank, checks permutation invariance, runs deterministic fibre searches,
and constructs distinct reset-preserving similarity equivalents with identical
visible tails. The saved output is
artifacts/verify_nstate_identifiability_output.txt.

Exact citations, arXiv API queries, DOI checks, and the restricted novelty
claim are recorded in artifacts/literature_check.md.

import unittest

import numpy as np

from artifacts import verify_nstate_identifiability as verify


class SerialKilledLeakageTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def test_exact_three_inclusion_image_equation(self):
        examples = (
            (0.35, 0.8, 0.2),
            (0.7, 1.6, 1.0),
            (2.0, 2.0, 1.0),
            (4.0, 0.45, 0.7),
        )
        for gamma, recovery, delta in examples:
            inclusions = verify.two_state_inclusion_coordinates(
                gamma, recovery, delta
            )
            residual = verify.physical_image_residual(inclusions)
            self.assertLess(abs(residual), 2e-12)

    def test_physical_image_equation_detects_intensity_perturbation(self):
        inclusions = verify.two_state_inclusion_coordinates(0.7, 1.6, 1.0)
        perturbed = inclusions.copy()
        perturbed[0] *= 1.01
        self.assertGreater(abs(verify.physical_image_residual(perturbed)), 1e-4)

    def test_hidden_mode_obeys_sharp_global_bound(self):
        grid = np.geomspace(1e-4, 50.0, 181)
        values = np.array(
            [verify.hidden_mode_secant(x, y) for x in grid for y in grid]
        )
        self.assertGreaterEqual(float(values.min()), -np.exp(-2.0) - 2e-14)
        self.assertLess(float(values.max()), 1.0)
        self.assertAlmostEqual(
            verify.hidden_mode_secant(2.0, 2.0), -np.exp(-2.0), places=15
        )

    def test_small_sampling_interval_mean_expansion_has_sixth_order_remainder(self):
        gamma = 0.7
        recovery = 1.6
        normalized_errors = []
        for delta in (0.2, 0.1, 0.05):
            exact = delta * verify.mean_cycle_length(gamma, recovery, delta)
            approximation = verify.small_delta_mean_expansion(
                gamma, recovery, delta
            )
            normalized_errors.append(abs(exact - approximation) / delta**6)
        self.assertLess(max(normalized_errors), 2e-3)

    def test_kernels_are_stochastic_and_clicks_reset(self):
        for rates in ((0.7, 1.6), (0.7, 1.2, 2.3)):
            t0, t1 = verify.serial_killed_reset_kernels(rates)
            np.testing.assert_allclose((t0 + t1).sum(axis=1), 1.0, atol=1e-13)
            self.assertGreaterEqual(float(t0.min()), -1e-14)
            self.assertGreaterEqual(float(t1.min()), -1e-14)
            self.assertTrue(np.allclose(t1[:, :-1], 0.0, atol=1e-14))

    def test_hankel_pencil_recovers_unordered_sampled_poles(self):
        for rates in ((0.7, 1.6), (0.7, 1.2, 2.3)):
            tails = verify.visible_tail_coordinates(rates, 2 * len(rates))
            recovered = verify.recover_sampled_poles(tails, len(rates))
            expected = np.sort(np.exp(-np.asarray(rates)))
            np.testing.assert_allclose(recovered, expected, rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-11)

    def test_confluent_recurrence_recovers_collision_multiplicities(self):
        examples = (
            (0.7, 0.7),
            (0.7, 1.2, 1.2),
            (0.7, 1.2, 1.2, 2.3),
        )
        for rates in examples:
            tails = verify.visible_tail_coordinates(rates, 3 * len(rates) + 1)
            polynomial, residual = verify.recover_minimal_recurrence(
                tails, len(rates)
            )
            expected = np.poly(np.exp(-np.asarray(rates, dtype=float)))
            np.testing.assert_allclose(
                polynomial, expected, rtol=2e-8, atol=2e-10
            )
            self.assertLess(residual, 2e-12)

    def test_collision_does_not_lower_serial_hankel_rank(self):
        examples = ((0.7, 0.7), (0.7, 1.2, 1.2), (0.7, 0.7, 2.3, 2.3))
        for rates in examples:
            tails = verify.visible_tail_coordinates(rates, 2 * len(rates))
            diagnostics = verify.hankel_diagnostics(tails, len(rates))
            self.assertEqual(diagnostics.rank, len(rates))
            self.assertGreater(diagnostics.smallest_singular_value, 1e-8)

    def test_visible_moments_are_permutation_invariant(self):
        rates = (0.45, 0.95, 1.8)
        baseline = verify.visible_click_moments(rates, 7)
        permuted = verify.visible_click_moments((1.8, 0.45, 0.95), 7)
        np.testing.assert_allclose(permuted, baseline, rtol=1e-12, atol=1e-13)

    def test_stochastic_similarity_changes_kernel_not_visible_law(self):
        examples = ((0.7, 1.6), (0.7, 1.2, 2.3), (0.7, 1.2, 1.2, 2.3))
        for rates in examples:
            t0, _ = verify.serial_killed_reset_kernels(rates)
            transformed = verify.equivalent_killed_reset_kernel(t0, epsilon=0.02)
            self.assertGreater(np.linalg.norm(transformed - t0), 1e-4)
            self.assertGreaterEqual(float(transformed.min()), -1e-13)
            base = verify.kernel_tail_coordinates(t0, 25)
            equivalent = verify.kernel_tail_coordinates(transformed, 25)
            np.testing.assert_allclose(equivalent, base, rtol=1e-11, atol=1e-12)

    def test_reset_preserving_similarity_tangent_has_expected_dimension(self):
        for n_states in (2, 3, 4):
            basis = verify.reset_similarity_lie_basis(n_states)
            self.assertEqual(len(basis), (n_states - 1) ** 2)
            reset = np.zeros(n_states)
            reset[-1] = 1.0
            for tangent in basis:
                np.testing.assert_allclose(tangent @ np.ones(n_states), 0.0)

\section{Higher-state fibres: recalled realization theory and a quantitative orbit theorem}

The minimal-realization statements in this subsection are recalled background,
not contributions of this paper.  Kalman's similarity theorem is the classical
source, and minimal MAP/phase-type formulations and canonical-coordinate
developments are given in
\cite{Kalman1963LinearSystems,TelekHorvath2007MinimalMAP,
BladtNielsen2017MatrixExponential,MeszarosTelek2013DiscreteMAP2Canonical,
PappTelek2013DiscretePHCanonical}.  We state the consequence needed to locate
the visible fibre, then prove the new quantitative assertion: at a minimal
interior killed-reset kernel the admissible fibre has local dimension
\((n-1)^2\).  Nonunique MAP and Coxian representatives are documented in
\cite{RamirezCoboLilloWiper2010MAP2Nonidentifiability,
RamirezCoboLillo2012WeakEquivalentMAP,RizkBurkeWalsh2019CoxianNonuniqueness}.
Graph-specific time-to-event inverses are treated algebraically by
Radulescu et al.\ \cite{RadulescuEtAl2025TimeToEventIdentifiability}; the
criterion below instead isolates the exact orbit fibre for any declared
minimal killed-reset subclass.

\paragraph{Recalled minimal-realization uniqueness.}
Let \((a,A,b)\) and \((\widetilde a,\widetilde A,\widetilde b)\) be two real
scalar realizations of the same dimension \(n\) such that
\[
aA^k b=\widetilde a\widetilde A^k\widetilde b
\qquad(k\ge0).
\]
Assume that both reachability matrices
\[
[\,b,Ab,\ldots,A^{n-1}b\,],\qquad
[\,\widetilde b,\widetilde A\widetilde b,\ldots,
\widetilde A^{n-1}\widetilde b\,]
\]
and both observability matrices
\[
\begin{bmatrix}a\\aA\\\vdots\\aA^{n-1}\end{bmatrix},
\qquad
\begin{bmatrix}\widetilde a\\\widetilde a\widetilde A\\\vdots\\
\widetilde a\widetilde A^{n-1}\end{bmatrix}
\]
have rank \(n\). Then there is a unique \(M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\RR)\)
such that
\[
\widetilde a=aM,
\qquad \widetilde A=M^{-1}AM,
\qquad \widetilde b=M^{-1}b.
\]
These rank hypotheses are precisely properties \textup{(R)} and \textup{(L)}
of Bladt and Nielsen, whose Theorem~4.2.16 characterizes minimality by their
simultaneous validity; the corresponding intertwining relations are given in
their Lemmas~4.2.5--4.2.6
\cite[Theorem~4.2.16, p.~216, and Lemmas~4.2.5--4.2.6,
p.~212]{BladtNielsen2017MatrixExponential}. This standard result is invoked
here and is not claimed as a new theorem; see also Kalman
\cite{Kalman1963LinearSystems}, Telek--Horv\'ath
\cite{TelekHorvath2007MinimalMAP}, and
\cite{Ryden1996Aggregated,OCinneide1989PhaseTypeNonuniqueness,
OCinneide1991InvariantPolytopes}.

\begin{proposition}[Recalled orbit-fibre consequence of minimal realization]
\label{thm:nstate-killed-reset-identifiability-dichotomy-main}
Fix \(n\ge2\), put \(\beta=e_n^\top\), and let
\[
\mathcal K_n=\{K\in\RR^{n\times n}:K\ge0,\ K\mathbf1\le\mathbf1,\
\operatorname{spr}(K)<1\}.
\]
For \(K\in\mathcal K_n\), define the killed-reset D-MAP by
\[
T_0=K,\qquad T_1=(I-K)\mathbf1\beta
\]
and its Palm survival coordinates by \(S_k(K)=\beta K^k\mathbf1\).
Call \(K\) minimal when both
\[
\mathcal C(K)=[\,\mathbf1,K\mathbf1,\ldots,K^{n-1}\mathbf1\,],
\qquad
\mathcal O(K)=
\begin{bmatrix}\beta\\ \beta K\\ \vdots\\ \beta K^{n-1}\end{bmatrix}
\]
have rank \(n\). Let
\[
\mathcal G_n=\{M\in\operatorname{GL}_n(\RR):
M\mathbf1=\mathbf1,\ \beta M=\beta\},
\]
and let \(\mathfrak P_n\subset\mathcal G_n\) be the reset-preserving
permutation matrices.

For any declared subclass \(\mathcal C\subset\mathcal K_n\) of minimal
kernels, fix the structural equivalence \(\sim_{\mathcal C}\) under which
identification is requested, and assume that \(K\sim_{\mathcal C}L\) implies
equality of visible laws. Examples are reset-preserving hidden-state
relabeling and, in a serial rate chart, permutation of the rate coordinates.
Define the Markovian orbit fibre
\[
\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}(K)=
\left\{M^{-1}KM\in\mathcal C:M\in\mathcal G_n\right\}
\big/\!\sim_{\mathcal C}.
\]
Then standard minimal-realization uniqueness gives the following exact
characterization.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Two minimal kernels \(K,L\in\mathcal K_n\) generate the same stationary
visible click law if and only if
\[
\begin{aligned}
L&=M^{-1}KM &&\text{for the unique }M\in\mathcal G_n\\
&&&\text{implementing their normalized minimal realizations}.
\end{aligned}
\]
\item Equivalently, the declared hidden object is identifiable from the visible law within
\(\mathcal C\), modulo \(\sim_{\mathcal C}\), if and only if
\[
\#\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}(K)=1\qquad\text{for every }K\in\mathcal C.
\]
Pointwise identifiability at \(K\) is equivalent to the same condition at
that \(K\); if the cardinality exceeds one, its distinct classes are exactly
the hidden nonidentifiability fibre. Thus this assertion is the orbit-fibre
reformulation of part \textup{(i)}.
\end{enumerate}
Part~\textup{(ii)} is deliberately recorded only as terminology: after the
fibre has been defined, singleton fibre and identifiability modulo
\(\sim_{\mathcal C}\) are the same assertion.  Neither part is claimed as a
new realization theorem.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Deterministic reset makes the visible process renewal. Its Palm gap tail is
exactly \(S_k(K)\), so equality of visible stationary laws is equivalent to
equality of all the scalar coordinates \(\beta K^k\mathbf1\), \(k\ge0\).
Apply the minimal-realization theorem stated above to the triples
\((\beta,K,\mathbf1)\) and \((\beta,L,\mathbf1)\). Its hypotheses are exactly
the two displayed rank conditions in the proposition, and it gives a unique
similarity \(L=M^{-1}KM\). Preservation of the fixed input and output vectors
gives \(M\mathbf1=\mathbf1\) and \(\beta M=\beta\), respectively.
Conversely, these two identities give
\[
\beta(M^{-1}KM)^k\mathbf1=\beta K^k\mathbf1
\]
for every \(k\), proving (i). Taking the intersection with
\(\mathcal C\) and then quotienting precisely the declared structural
equivalence proves
the necessary-and-sufficient assertion (ii).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[All-collision serial identifiability]
\label{cor:nstate-serial-all-collision-identifiability-main}
Fix \(n\ge2\), a known \(\Delta\tau>0\), and arbitrary positive rates
\(\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\), with repetitions allowed. Let
\[
Q(\theta)_{ii}=-\theta_i,\qquad
Q(\theta)_{i,i-1}=\theta_i\quad(2\le i\le n),
\]
with all other entries zero, and put
\[
T_0(\theta)=e^{\Delta\tau Q(\theta)},\qquad
T_1(\theta)=(I-T_0(\theta))\mathbf1e_n^\top.
\]
Then the visible record identifies exactly the unordered rate multiset
\(\{\!\{\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n\}\!\}\). Equivalently, the fibre of the
labelled serial parameter is its \(\mathfrak S_n\)-permutation orbit.

More explicitly, if the distinct rates are
\(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_r\) with multiplicities
\(m_1,\ldots,m_r\), and \(z_j=e^{-\lambda_j\Delta\tau}\), then the Palm tail
has the confluent Prony form
\[
S_k=\sum_{j=1}^r\sum_{\ell=0}^{m_j-1}
c_{j\ell}k^\ell z_j^k,\qquad c_{j,m_j-1}\ne0,
\]
and its minimal recurrence polynomial is
\[
\chi_\theta(x)=\prod_{j=1}^r(x-z_j)^{m_j}.
\]
The leading \(n\times n\) Hankel matrix
\((S_{i+j})_{0\le i,j<n}\) is invertible; hence
\(S_0,\ldots,S_{2n-1}\) determine \(\chi_\theta\), including all collision
multiplicities. Pole collision therefore changes conditioning and the local
root chart, but does not change population identifiability.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Starting in phase \(n\), the absorption time is
\(W=X_n+\cdots+X_1\), where the \(X_i\) are independent exponentials with
rates \(\theta_i\). Its Laplace transform is
\[
\EE e^{-sW}=\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{\theta_i}{s+\theta_i}.
\]
Consequently
\[
\int_0^\infty e^{-st}\PP(W>t)\,dt
=\frac{1-\prod_{i=1}^n\theta_i/(s+\theta_i)}{s}
\]
has at
\(-\lambda_j\) a pole of exact order \(m_j\). Partial-fraction inversion and
sampling at \(t=k\Delta\tau\) give the displayed exponential-polynomial form
with nonzero top confluent coefficient. Standard confluent Prony algebra
then gives the exact minimal annihilator \(\chi_\theta\)
\cite{KunisRoemerVonDerOhe2020Prony}.

For completeness of the finite-coordinate assertion, the matrices
\(\mathcal O(Q)\) and \(\mathcal C(Q)\) are nonsingular: successive rows
\(e_n^\top Q^j\) and successive columns \(Q^j\mathbf1\) expose the nonzero
bidiagonal products triangularly. Because the exponential is injective on
the real spectrum of \(Q\), Hermite interpolation supplies a polynomial
\(p\) with \(Q=p(e^{\Delta\tau Q})\); hence the corresponding observation and
reachability spaces for \(T_0=e^{\Delta\tau Q}\) are also full. Therefore
\[
(S_{i+j})_{0\le i,j<n}=\mathcal O(T_0)\mathcal C(T_0)
\]
is invertible, and the first \(2n\) tails solve uniquely for the order-\(n\)
recurrence. The roots and their algebraic multiplicities recover
\(\lambda_j=-\Delta\tau^{-1}\log z_j\) and \(m_j\). Conversely, permuting
the independent summands does not change \(W\), the Palm gap law, or the
stationary renewal law. This proves the exact fibre claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Quantitative interior fibre dimension and positivity persistence]
\label{thm:nstate-interior-continuum-nonidentifiability-main}
For the unrestricted class with \(\sim_{\mathcal K_n}\) equal to
reset-preserving state relabelling, the hidden kernel is locally
nonidentifiable at every minimal interior point \(K\), where interior means
\(K>0\) and \((I-K)\mathbf1>0\) entrywise. More precisely, the
reset-preserving similarity group has Lie algebra
\[
\mathfrak g_n=\{B:B\mathbf1=0,\ \beta B=0\},
\qquad \dim\mathfrak g_n=(n-1)^2,
\]
and the orbit map
\[
\psi_K:\mathcal G_n\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{n\times n},\qquad
\psi_K(M)=M^{-1}KM,
\]
has injective differential
\[
D\psi_K(I)B=[K,B]\qquad(B\in\mathfrak g_n).
\]
Consequently the visible fibre through \(K\) contains, in a neighbourhood of
\(K\), a smooth immersed manifold of dimension exactly \((n-1)^2\).  Every
kernel on a sufficiently small neighbourhood of this orbit manifold remains
strictly substochastic: its entries and killing deficits are positive.  After
quotienting by the finite reset-preserving permutation group, the local fibre
still has dimension \((n-1)^2\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Because \(\beta\mathbf1=1\),
\(\RR^n=\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf1\}\oplus\ker\beta\).  Relative to this
decomposition, \(B\mathbf1=0\) removes the first block column and
\(\beta B=0\) forces the range into \(\ker\beta\).  Thus
\(B=\operatorname{diag}(0,A)\), with arbitrary
\(A\in\operatorname{End}(\ker\beta)\), and
\(\dim\mathfrak g_n=(n-1)^2\).

Differentiating \(\exp(-tB)K\exp(tB)\) at zero gives
\(D\psi_K(I)B=[K,B]\).  Suppose \([K,B]=0\).  Since \(B\mathbf1=0\),
\[
BK^j\mathbf1=K^jB\mathbf1=0,
\qquad j=0,\ldots,n-1.
\]
The reachability matrix
\([\mathbf1,K\mathbf1,\ldots,K^{n-1}\mathbf1]\) has rank \(n\), so these
equalities imply \(B=0\).  Hence the differential is injective on all of
\(\mathfrak g_n\), not merely in one selected direction.

The constant-rank theorem now makes the image of \(\psi_K\) near the identity
a smooth immersed manifold of dimension \((n-1)^2\).  For every
\(M\in\mathcal G_n\),
\[
\beta\psi_K(M)^j\mathbf1=\beta K^j\mathbf1\qquad(j\ge0),
\]
so the recalled orbit-fibre result places this entire manifold in the visible
fibre.  Finally, all entries of \(M^{-1}KM\) and all components of
\((I-M^{-1}KM)\mathbf1\) depend continuously on \(M\).  Their values at
\(M=I\) are strictly positive; a sufficiently small identity neighbourhood
therefore remains inside the interior Markovian cone.  The stabilizer has zero
Lie algebra by injectivity of the differential, and quotienting by the finite
reset-preserving permutation group cannot change local dimension.  This proves
all assertions.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Nonminimal and graph-specific open interfaces]
\label{rem:nstate-identifiability-open-interfaces-main}
The characterization and the two headline results deliberately assume
Hankel/minimal rank \(n\). If a nominal
\(n\)-state representation has lower visible rank, equal laws need not be
related by an invertible \(n\times n\) similarity; a sharp classification then
requires a stratified treatment of nonminimal augmentations. For a fixed
nonserial zero pattern on the boundary of the Markovian cone, evaluating the
orbit intersection \(\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}(K)\) is an exact semialgebraic
problem, but no graph-uniform closed form is claimed here. Finally, collision
multiplicity is population-identifiable in the serial model but statistically
singular under noisy finite records. These are explicit interfaces, not
consequences of the present results.
\end{remark}

For orientation, the unrestricted fibre is already nontrivial in two states:
\[
K=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\1/2&1/4\end{pmatrix},\qquad
M=\begin{pmatrix}9/10&1/10\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
M^{-1}KM=\begin{pmatrix}9/20&1/45\\9/20&3/10\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Both kernels are nonnegative and substochastic,
\(M\mathbf1=\mathbf1\), \(e_2^\top M=e_2^\top\), and their entire visible
renewal laws coincide, although the hidden kernels do not.
